passages.title: Air Travel vs. the Environment
passages.subtitle: Balancing budget flights, tourism jobs, and rising carbon emissions
paragraphs: Fifty years ago, flying abroad was a rare luxury reserved for wealthy businesspeople and movie stars. Today, the rise of budget airlines has made air travel affordable for millions of ordinary families. Cheap weekend tickets allow young people to explore foreign capitals, visit distant relatives, and enjoy greater travel freedom than any earlier generation.

Yet flying has a heavy impact on the planet. Per passenger kilometre, aeroplanes release far more carbon emissions than trains or shared buses, and even more than a car carrying a full family. Because planes burn jet fuel high in the atmosphere, their warm exhaust trails trap extra heat, making aviation one of the fastest-growing sources of climate pollution.

In response, environmental campaigners want governments to limit non-essential flights, especially short domestic trips where fast trains already exist. France, for example, recently banned short-haul domestic flights on routes that can be completed in under two and a half hours by rail. Some campaigners also call for higher ticket taxes on frequent flyers to discourage unnecessary weekend trips.

However, raising flight prices sharply could hurt the tourism industry and international business. Many island nations and coastal towns depend heavily on holidaymakers arriving by plane to support local hotels, cafes, and tour guides. Business groups also warn that making flights too expensive could reduce global trade and unfairly limit travel freedom for lower-income families.

Many airlines now promote a simple three-step 'carbon offset' process for passengers who still need to fly. First, travellers calculate the CO2 from their journey using an online calculator on the booking website. Next, passengers pay a small extra fee to fund green projects such as planting trees or building solar farms. Finally, independent auditors check these projects to confirm they genuinely absorb carbon—though critics warn that paying to offset is never as good as simply taking fewer flights and investing in cleaner electric or biofuel aircraft.

passages.title: Cleaner Cities: From Car-Free Days to Cycling
passages.subtitle: How urban leaders tackle traffic congestion and air pollution through sustainable transport
paragraphs: 1 Every morning in major cities around the world, millions of drivers sit trapped in slow-moving lines of cars. Heavy traffic congestion wastes hours of workers' lives and fills city streets with dangerous air pollution that causes asthma and heart illness. To reclaim urban roads for people, mayors from Paris to Bogota are experimenting with bold new ways to encourage sustainable transport.

2 One popular idea is holding a regular car-free day. Every Sunday in Bogota, Colombia, over 120 kilometres of main avenues are closed to motor vehicles, turning noisy highways into safe spaces for walkers, runners, and families on bicycles. Similarly, annual vehicle-free days in European capitals allow residents to experience how quiet and pleasant their neighbourhoods feel without engines.

3 Critics argue that a single car-free Sunday does not change weekday habits. However, city planners say these events act as a powerful showcase: once citizens enjoy cleaner air and safer streets, they are much more willing to support permanent changes during their Monday-to-Friday commute.

4 Encouraging everyday cycling is one of the cheapest and healthiest ways to cut transport emissions. In Dutch cities like Utrecht and Amsterdam, wide separated cycle lanes, smooth pavements, and giant bicycle garages near train stations make riding a bike the fastest way to cross town. As a result, people of all ages—from schoolchildren to grandparents—cycle comfortably in regular clothes.

5 Still, cycling is not easy everywhere. In many cities, commuters face real barriers: narrow roads with no safe cycle lanes, heavy rain or extreme summer heat, steep hills, and fear of careless drivers. Elderly people and residents carrying heavy groceries also cannot rely on bicycles alone.

6 For this reason, successful clean cities combine safe bike networks with fast, affordable public transport. Adding electric buses, clean subways, and shaded walking paths ensures that every resident—regardless of age or weather—has a safe, low-carbon way to move around town.

passages.label: READING PASSAGE 3

passages.title: Waste, Recycling and Plastic
passages.subtitle: Tackling food waste, low recycling rates, and single-use plastic pollution
paragraphs: 1 Every year, cities around the globe produce over two billion tonnes of household rubbish. Much of this waste is dumped into giant open sites called landfill, where rotting trash releases methane—a powerful greenhouse gas—and leaks dirty liquids into underground water. Reducing rubbish has become one of the most urgent environmental tasks of our time.

2 Two categories of waste cause special concern: food waste and plastic. Around one-third of all food grown in the world is never eaten, thrown away by supermarkets that reject ugly vegetables or by households that buy too much. Meanwhile, single-use plastic—such as shopping bags, drink bottles, and food wrappers—has created severe plastic pollution in rivers and oceans, harming turtles, seabirds, and fish.

3 Recycling seems like an obvious answer, yet the global recycling rate for plastic remains shockingly low—under ten percent. Many citizens feel confused about which bin takes which material, and a single dirty food container can spoil an entire truckload of clean paper or plastic. In addition, making brand-new plastic from cheap oil often costs factories less than sorting and cleaning old plastic.

4 Because voluntary recycling has moved too slowly, many governments are introducing strict laws. Over ninety countries now place a partial or total ban on lightweight plastic shopping bags, encouraging shoppers to carry cloth totes instead. In South Korea and Germany, strict sorting laws require families to separate food scraps, glass, and paper into different bins, and local authorities impose fines on households or businesses that break the rules.

5 Laws work even better when paired with education from an early age. In Japanese primary schools, children learn to wash milk cartons, sort classroom rubbish, and finish all the food on their lunch trays every day. Community campaigns also raise awareness about 'best-before' dates so families stop throwing away fresh food unnecessarily.

6 Ultimately, recycling alone cannot save us if we keep producing mountains of throwaway items. Combining strict plastic bans, fair fines, smart supermarket rules, and childhood education can turn wasteful cities into cleaner, smarter communities that respect every resource.
